title: How to Talk to Your Kids About Sex
excerpt: The sex talk is not a single dreaded event but a long, ordinary conversation. If you do not have it, the culture and the search bar will have it for you.
body:
Many Christian parents are still waiting for the right moment to have the talk, and the right moment passed years ago. By the time you sit your child down for the formal version, they have already absorbed a hundred messages from screens, friends, and a culture that is not shy. The question was never whether your child would learn about sex. The question is whether you would be one of the voices they learned from, or the one voice that stayed silent.

Silence is not neutrality. Silence teaches that this is shameful, that the parents cannot be asked, that the answers must be found elsewhere. That is the opposite of what you want.

## Make it a conversation, not an event

The single most freeing shift is this: it is not one talk. It is dozens of small, low-stakes conversations spread across years. A toddler asks where babies come from and you give a true, simple answer. A seven-year-old hears a word on the bus and you explain it plainly. A twelve-year-old's body starts changing and you are already someone they can ask.

This takes the pressure off the dreaded sit-down. You are not delivering one terrifying lecture. You are being askable, over and over, until your child knows that no question will shock you out of the room.

## Use real words and a calm face

Use the actual names for body parts from the beginning. Coded language teaches shame before you have said anything about it. A parent who can name the body without flinching tells a child that this is good, made by God, and not dirty.

Genesis says God made us male and female and called it very good. The Song of Songs puts an entire book of married desire in the canon without apology. The Christian story does not treat the body as an embarrassment. Your face should match that theology. When your child asks something, the goal is a calm, unstartled answer, even when your insides are doing something else.

## Give the meaning, not just the mechanics

The culture is happy to teach your children the mechanics. What it will not teach them is what sex is for. This is the part only you can give.

Tell them sex is not shameful and not casual. It is a covenant act, a sign of a promise, the kind of self-giving that belongs inside a love that has bound itself for life. Frame it as something honored, not something forbidden. "Wait" lands very differently when it means "this is too good to spend cheaply" than when it means "this is dirty and dangerous." One produces freedom. The other produces shame, and shame does not actually keep anyone pure. It just keeps them quiet.

## Talk about what they will actually encounter

Name the things they will meet, before they meet them. They will see pornography, probably younger than you would guess and probably by accident first. Tell them now what it is and why it lies about sex, that it shows bodies without persons and pleasure without covenant. Tell them that if they stumble into it, or go looking and feel ashamed, they can come to you, and you will not detonate.

This is the hardest promise to keep and the most important. The child who believes a parent will react with horror is the child who hides everything. Be the one they can tell. Your steadiness when they confess is worth more than any rule you could enforce.

## Stay ahead of the changing body

Do not let puberty arrive as a surprise that nobody warned them about. A child whose body starts changing without a single honest word from a parent assumes something is wrong with them, or that this too belongs in the category of the unspeakable. Talk about it before it happens, plainly and matter-of-factly, so that when it comes they meet it as something expected and good rather than alarming and shameful. The body God designed is doing exactly what it was made to do, and your child should hear that from you first.

## Match your words to their age

What you say at five is not what you say at fifteen, and trying to deliver the whole truth at once either overwhelms a small child or arrives years too late for an older one. Give a little child a simple, true, age-sized answer to the question they actually asked, no more. Give an older child the fuller picture, including the parts that are harder and the parts the world will lie to them about. The conversation grows with the child, which is one more reason it cannot be a single talk. It is a relationship that stays open as the child changes.

## This week

Decide that you are the one who will talk about this, and then lower the stakes. You do not need a perfect speech. You need to be askable. The next time your child raises anything close to the subject, however awkwardly, answer plainly, calmly, and without ending the conversation. If nothing comes up naturally this week, find one small opening yourself, suited to their age, and prove to them with one ordinary conversation that this door is open. Then keep it open for the next ten years.
